entries.lesson_core_move: Identify the nonzero interval of $x(\tau)$ in the convolution variable so it becomes the fixed support constraint for determining overlap with $h(t-\tau)$.

sections.section_title: Reading the Support of a Basic Signal in $\tau$

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$ if $x(\tau)=5$ for $-2\le \tau\le 1$ and $x(\tau)=0$ otherwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is nonzero exactly on $-2\le \tau\le 1$. The amplitude $5$ does not change the support, so the support is $[-2,1]$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$ if $x(\tau)=-3$ for $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $x(\tau)=0$ otherwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support is the interval where $x(\tau)$ is nonzero. Since $x(\tau)=-3$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and is zero otherwise, the support is $[0,4]$.

sections.section_title: Finding Support from a Piecewise Definition in $\tau$

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The zero branches cover $\tau<-3$ and $\tau>0$. The only active branch is $4-\tau$ on $-3\le \tau\le 0$, so that branch condition is the support.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The first and last branches are exactly zero, so they are outside the support. The nonzero branch is $\tau+6$ on $-4\le \tau\le -1$, which gives the support interval.

sections.section_title: Finding Support from Unit Step Windows in $\tau$

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The unit step $u(\tau+2)$ turns on at $\tau=-2$, and subtracting $u(\tau-1)$ turns the window off at $\tau=1$. The factor $\tau^2+1$ is nonzero on that window, so the support is $-2\le \tau\le 1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the support of $x(\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The window starts when $u(\tau+4)$ turns on at $\tau=-4$ and ends when the subtracted step $u(\tau+1)$ turns on at $\tau=-1$. Since $e^{2\tau}$ is nonzero for every $\tau$, the support is $-4\le \tau\le -1$.

sections.section_title: Writing the Fixed Support Constraint for $x(\tau)$

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $-1\le \tau\le 4$, write the fixed support constraint for $x(\tau)$ that will be used when finding overlap with $h(t-\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support has already been identified. To write it as the fixed support constraint, keep the variable as $\tau$ and copy the endpoints: $-1\le \tau\le 4$. No $t$ appears, so this is the fixed constraint from $x(\tau)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given that $\operatorname{supp} x=[-6,-2]$, write the fixed support constraint for $x(\tau)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[-6,-2]$ means $x(\tau)$ is nonzero from $\tau=-6$ through $\tau=-2$. Written as the fixed support constraint, this is $-6\le \tau\le -2$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the support interval of $h(u)$ into the corresponding interval for $h(t-\tau)$ by holding $t$ fixed and reversing the inequalities in $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Holding $t$ Fixed in the Support Condition for $h(t-\tau)$

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-2 \le u \le 1$. For fixed $t=5$, what is the support of $h(t-\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Hold $t=5$ fixed and substitute $u=5-\tau$: $-2 \le 5-\tau \le 1$. Subtracting $5$ gives $-7 \le -\tau \le -4$, and multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequalities, so $4 \le \tau \le 7$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $1 \le u \le 4$. For fixed $t=6$, what is the support of $h(t-\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: With $t=6$, the support condition becomes $1 \le 6-\tau \le 4$. Subtracting $6$ gives $-5 \le -\tau \le -2$; multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequalities, giving $2 \le \tau \le 5$.

sections.section_title: Converting an $h(u)$ Support Interval into an Inequality for $t-\tau$

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-2 \le u \le 5$. Which inequality gives the support condition for $h(t-\tau)$ before isolating $\tau$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The argument of $h$ is $t-\tau$, so replace $u$ with $t-\tau$ and keep the same support endpoints. The pre-isolation support condition is $-2 \le t-\tau \le 5$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-6 \le u \le -1$. Which inequality gives the support condition for $h(t-\tau)$ before isolating $\tau$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support interval tells when the input to $h$ is between $-6$ and $-1$. For $h(t-\tau)$, that input is $t-\tau$, so the condition is $-6 \le t-\tau \le -1$ before any solving for $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Reversing Inequalities to Isolate $\tau$

prompt_blocks.text: Given the support condition $-1 \le t-\tau \le 3$, which interval gives the values of $\tau$ for which $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Subtract $t$ from all three parts to get $-1-t \le -\tau \le 3-t$. Multiplying by $-1$ reverses both inequalities, giving $t+1 \ge \tau \ge t-3$, which is $t-3 \le \tau \le t+1$ in increasing $\tau$ order.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the support condition $4 \le t-\tau \le 7$, which interval gives the values of $\tau$ for which $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Subtracting $t$ gives $4-t \le -\tau \le 7-t$. Multiplying by $-1$ reverses both inequality signs, so $t-4 \ge \tau \ge t-7$. Written in increasing $\tau$ order, the interval is $t-7 \le \tau \le t-4$.

sections.section_title: Writing the $h(t-\tau)$ Support Interval in Increasing $\tau$ Order

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-3 \le u \le 2$. Which interval is the support of $h(t-\tau)$ written in increasing $\tau$ order?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert the support to $-3 \le t-\tau \le 2$. Solving for $\tau$ gives $t+3 \ge \tau \ge t-2$, so the increasing-order interval is $t-2 \le \tau \le t+3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-4 \le u \le 1$. Which interval is the support of $h(t-\tau)$ written in increasing $\tau$ order?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support condition is $-4 \le t-\tau \le 1$. After isolating $\tau$, the endpoints are $t+4$ and $t-1$; the smaller endpoint is $t-1$, so the increasing-order support interval is $t-1 \le \tau \le t+4$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows $h(u)$ supported on $1 \le u \le 4$ and the corresponding flip-shift picture for $h(t-\tau)$. Which $\tau$ interval matches the moving support?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $h(t-\tau)$, the right endpoint of the original support maps to the left endpoint: $u=4$ gives $\tau=t-4$. The left endpoint maps to the right endpoint: $u=1$ gives $\tau=t-1$. So the moving support is $t-4 \le \tau \le t-1$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows $h(u)$ supported on $-2 \le u \le 3$ and the corresponding flip-shift picture for $h(t-\tau)$. Which $\tau$ interval matches the moving support?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The endpoint order reverses for $h(t-\tau)$. The original right endpoint $u=3$ maps to $\tau=t-3$, and the original left endpoint $u=-2$ maps to $\tau=t+2$. Thus the moving support is $t-3 \le \tau \le t+2$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Intersect the support of $x(\tau)$ with the support of $h(t-\tau)$ for a fixed $t$ to determine where the convolution integrand is nonzero.

sections.section_title: Intersecting Supports for One Fixed $t$

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $-1 \le \tau \le 3$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-2 \le \tau \le t+1$. Determine the overlap interval when $t=1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $t=1$ into the moving support for $h(t-\tau)$.
Intersect this with the fixed support $-1 \le \tau \le 3$. The larger lower endpoint is $-1$, and the smaller upper endpoint is $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $-3 \le \tau \le 2$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-5 \le \tau \le t-1$. Determine the overlap interval when $t=3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $t=3$ into the moving support interval for $h(t-\tau)$.
Now intersect $-3 \le \tau \le 2$ with $-2 \le \tau \le 2$. The larger lower endpoint is $-2$, and the smaller upper endpoint is $2$.

sections.section_title: Writing Overlap with Lower and Upper Endpoint Rules

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $-2 \le \tau \le 2$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-1 \le \tau \le t+3$. Write the overlap interval using lower- and upper-endpoint rules.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower endpoints are $-2$ and $t-1$, so the overlap starts at their maximum. The upper endpoints are $2$ and $t+3$, so the overlap ends at their minimum.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $1 \le \tau \le 6$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-4 \le \tau \le t+2$. Write the overlap interval using lower- and upper-endpoint rules.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The overlap must satisfy both support intervals. Use the larger lower endpoint, $\max(1,t-4)$, and the smaller upper endpoint, $\min(6,t+2)$.

sections.section_title: Finding the $t$ Values Where Endpoint Order Changes

prompt_blocks.text: For the endpoint-rule overlap $\max(-1,t-4) \le \tau \le \min(3,t+1)$, find the $t$ values where the lower endpoint choice or upper endpoint choice can change.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower endpoint can change when the two expressions inside the maximum are equal: $-1=t-4$, so $t=3$. The upper endpoint can change when the two expressions inside the minimum are equal: $3=t+1$, so $t=2$.

prompt_blocks.text: For the endpoint-rule overlap $\max(2,t+1) \le \tau \le \min(7,t+4)$, find the $t$ values where the lower endpoint choice or upper endpoint choice can change.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare only the competing endpoints inside each max or min. For the lower endpoint, $2=t+1$ gives $t=1$. For the upper endpoint, $7=t+4$ gives $t=3$.

sections.section_title: Determining Overlap Intervals Across Time Regions

prompt_blocks.text: For the active overlap range $-2 \le t \le 7$, suppose the endpoint-rule overlap is $\max(-1,t-4) \le \tau \le \min(3,t+1)$. Determine the overlap interval in each time region where the endpoint formulas differ.

questions.correct_answer: For $-2 \le t \le 2$: $-1 \le \tau \le t+1$; for $2 \le t \le 3$: $-1 \le \tau \le 3$; for $3 \le t \le 7$: $t-4 \le \tau \le 3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The endpoint choices can change when $-1=t-4$, giving $t=3$, and when $3=t+1$, giving $t=2$. These values split the active range into three regions.

prompt_blocks.text: For the active overlap range $0 \le t \le 6$, suppose the endpoint-rule overlap is $\max(1,t-2) \le \tau \le \min(5,t+1)$. Determine the overlap interval in each time region where the endpoint formulas differ.

questions.correct_answer: For $0 \le t \le 3$: $1 \le \tau \le t+1$; for $3 \le t \le 4$: $t-2 \le \tau \le t+1$; for $4 \le t \le 6$: $t-2 \le \tau \le 5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower endpoint changes where $1=t-2$, so $t=3$. The upper endpoint changes where $5=t+1$, so $t=4$. Use those values to partition the active range.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate the overlap interval into the lower and upper $\tau$ limits for the continuous-time convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds from a Constant Overlap Interval

prompt_blocks.text: Given that the overlap interval is $-1 \le \tau \le 2$, write the convolution integral bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ on that time region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The overlap interval has lower endpoint $-1$ and upper endpoint $2$, so those become the lower and upper limits of integration.
The integrand stays unchanged; this step only sets the constant bounds.

prompt_blocks.text: The overlap interval is $[0,4]$ in the variable $\tau$. Write the bounded convolution integral for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ on that time region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval notation $[0,4]$ means $0 \le \tau \le 4$, so $0$ is the lower limit and $4$ is the upper limit.
Nothing is evaluated and the integration variable remains $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds with a $t$-Dependent Lower Limit

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the overlap interval is $t-4 \le \tau \le 2$, write the corresponding convolution integral bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the overlap interval from left to right in the $\tau$ variable. The lower endpoint is $t-4$, and the upper endpoint is $2$.
The expression $t-4$ stays in the lower limit because integration is with respect to $\tau$, with $t$ held fixed.

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the nonempty overlap interval is $t+1 \le \tau \le 5$, write the bounded convolution integral for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The overlap interval gives the bounds directly: $t+1$ is the lower endpoint and $5$ is the constant upper endpoint.
This step only places the overlap endpoints as limits; the integrand is unchanged and the integral is not evaluated.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds with a $t$-Dependent Upper Limit

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the overlap interval is $-1 \le \tau \le t-2$, write the corresponding convolution integral bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the overlap interval in increasing $\tau$ order. The constant endpoint $-1$ is the lower limit, and the endpoint $t-2$ is the upper limit.
The $t$-dependent endpoint stays in the upper-limit position because integration is with respect to $\tau$.

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the nonempty overlap interval is $2 \le \tau \le t+3$, write the bounded convolution integral for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The left endpoint of the overlap interval is $2$, so it becomes the lower limit. The right endpoint is $t+3$, so it becomes the upper limit.
This step only sets the bounds; the integrand remains $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ and the integral is not evaluated.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds When Both Limits Depend on $t$

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the overlap interval is $t-5 \le \tau \le t-2$, write the corresponding convolution integral bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the endpoints directly from the overlap inequality. The lower endpoint is $t-5$, and the upper endpoint is $t-2$.
Do not cancel the $t$ terms or replace the limits with a width; the endpoint expressions stay as the limits of integration.

prompt_blocks.text: On a time region where the overlap interval is $t-1 \le \tau \le t+3$, write the bounded convolution integral for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The expression on the left of the $\tau$ inequality, $t-1$, becomes the lower limit. The expression on the right, $t+3$, becomes the upper limit.
Since the integral is with respect to $\tau$, $t$ is held fixed and both $t$-dependent endpoints remain in the bounds.

sections.section_title: Writing Region-Specific Integrals from Overlap Bounds

prompt_blocks.text: Given the overlap intervals below, write the corresponding region-specific convolution integrals for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Treat each time region as its own case and convert that region's overlap endpoints directly into integration limits.
The two regions should not be merged, and neither integral should be evaluated.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the overlap intervals below, write the corresponding region-specific convolution integrals for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Each stated time region keeps its own overlap interval. Use the left endpoint as the lower limit and the right endpoint as the upper limit in that same row.
The integrand remains unchanged in all cases; only the bounds and matching time regions change.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate the convolution integral separately on each time region where the overlap bounds change, then assemble the piecewise output.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the First Overlap Region

prompt_blocks.text: For $0 \le t \le 2$, evaluate the first-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Integrate with respect to $\tau$, treating $t$ as fixed. The antiderivative of $3$ is $3\tau$.
So the first overlap region gives $y(t)=3t$ for $0 \le t \le 2$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $0 \le t \le 4$, evaluate the first-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Integrate with respect to $\tau$, treating $t$ as fixed. The antiderivative of $2$ is $2\tau$.
So the first overlap region gives $y(t)=2t$ for $0 \le t \le 4$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Middle Region with New Bounds

prompt_blocks.text: For $2 \le t \le 4$, evaluate the middle-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is a middle region, so use the fixed bounds $0$ and $2$ rather than reusing an upper bound of $t$.
So the middle overlap region gives $y(t)=4$ for $2 \le t \le 4$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $3 \le t \le 5$, evaluate the middle-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The bounds are fixed on this middle region, so the result is a constant regional value. Integrate with respect to $\tau$.
So the middle overlap region gives $y(t)=6$ for $3 \le t \le 5$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Last Overlap Region

prompt_blocks.text: For $3 \le t \le 5$, evaluate the last-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower bound depends on $t$, so substitute upper minus lower carefully after integrating with respect to $\tau$.
So the last overlap region gives $y(t)=10-2t$ for $3 \le t \le 5$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $4 \le t \le 6$, evaluate the last-region convolution integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Treat $t$ as fixed while integrating with respect to $\tau$. The upper bound is $2$, and the moving lower bound is $t-4$.
So the last overlap region gives $y(t)=18-3t$ for $4 \le t \le 6$.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Convolution Output

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t)=2t$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, $y(t)=2$ for $1 \le t \le 3$, and $y(t)=8-2t$ for $3 \le t \le 4$, assemble the nonzero piecewise convolution output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep each evaluated regional formula attached to its original interval and list the intervals in increasing order of $t$. Do not add outside zero-output regions because the prompt asks only for the nonzero output.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t)=3t$ for $0 \le t \le 2$, $y(t)=6$ for $2 \le t \le 4$, and $y(t)=18-3t$ for $4 \le t \le 6$, assemble the nonzero piecewise convolution output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The three formulas are already evaluated; assembly means preserving the formula-interval pairs under one piecewise definition in increasing $t$ order.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify values of $t$ where the supports of $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ do not overlap, and set the convolution output to zero on those regions.

sections.section_title: Recognizing No Overlap Before the Moving Support Reaches $x(\tau)$

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $2\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-3\le \tau\le t-1$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap before the moving support reaches $x(\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Before contact, the moving interval must be entirely to the left of the fixed interval. Compare the moving right endpoint $t-1$ with the fixed left endpoint $2$: $t-1<2$, so $t<3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-5\le \tau\le t-2$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap before the moving support reaches $x(\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Before the moving support reaches $x(\tau)$, its right endpoint must still be less than the fixed support's left endpoint. Here the moving right endpoint is $t-2$ and the fixed left endpoint is $0$, so $t-2<0$, which gives $t<2$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing No Overlap After the Moving Support Passes $x(\tau)$

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-4\le \tau\le t-1$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap after the moving support passes $x(\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: After the moving support passes $x(\tau)$, compare the moving left endpoint with the fixed right endpoint. Here that gives $t-4>3$, so $t>7$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $-2\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-3\le \tau\le t+1$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap after the moving support passes $x(\tau)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For after-contact no overlap, the moving interval must start to the right of the fixed interval. The moving left endpoint is $t-3$ and the fixed right endpoint is $2$, so $t-3>2$, which gives $t>5$.

sections.section_title: Finding All Zero-Output Regions from Support Endpoints

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-3\le \tau\le t+1$. Which $t$-regions give zero convolution output because the supports do not overlap?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: There are two outside zero-output regions. Before contact, compare the moving right endpoint with the fixed left endpoint: $t+1<0$, so $t<-1$. After contact, compare the moving left endpoint with the fixed right endpoint: $t-3>4$, so $t>7$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $-2\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-1\le \tau\le t+2$. Which $t$-regions make $(x*h)(t)=0$ because the supports do not overlap?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Before contact, the moving right endpoint must be less than the fixed left endpoint: $t+2<-2$, so $t<-4$. After contact, the moving left endpoint must be greater than the fixed right endpoint: $t-1>5$, so $t>6$. Combining the outside regions gives $t<-4$ or $t>6$.

sections.section_title: Adding Zero-Output Regions to a Piecewise Convolution

prompt_blocks.text: A convolution has nonzero overlap only for $0<t<6$, with evaluated pieces already assigned as $y_1(t)$ on $0<t<3$ and $y_2(t)$ on $3\le t<6$. Which piecewise statement correctly adds the zero-output regions?

questions.correct_answer: $(x*h)(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $t\ge 6$, with $y_1(t)$ on $0<t<3$ and $y_2(t)$ on $3\le t<6$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The nonzero-overlap interval is only $0<t<6$, so the zero-output regions are the outside regions $t\le 0$ and $t\ge 6$. The already evaluated pieces stay on $0<t<3$ and $3\le t<6$.

prompt_blocks.text: A convolution has nonzero overlap only for $-1<t<8$, with evaluated pieces already assigned as $g_1(t)$ on $-1<t<2$ and $g_2(t)$ on $2\le t<8$. Which piecewise statement correctly adds the zero-output regions?

questions.correct_answer: $(x*h)(t)=0$ for $t\le -1$ and $t\ge 8$, with $g_1(t)$ on $-1<t<2$ and $g_2(t)$ on $2\le t<8$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The full nonzero-overlap interval is $-1<t<8$, so the convolution is zero before that interval and after that interval: $t\le -1$ and $t\ge 8$. The internal breakpoint $t=2$ only separates the existing nonzero pieces.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply commutativity to swap the convolution factors when doing so makes the support analysis, overlap bounds, or piecewise evaluation simpler.

sections.section_title: Swapping the Factors in a Convolution Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite the convolution integral using commutativity so that $a(\tau)$ is the fixed factor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In the original form, $b(\tau)$ is the fixed factor and $a(t-\tau)$ is the shifted factor. To make $a(\tau)$ fixed, swap the factors using commutativity while keeping $t$ as the output variable and $\tau$ as the integration variable.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite the convolution integral using commutativity so that $g(\tau)$ is the fixed factor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The original integral fixes $f(\tau)$ and shifts $g(t-\tau)$. Commutativity lets us swap the roles, so $g$ becomes $g(\tau)$ and $f$ becomes $f(t-\tau)$; the output remains $r(t)$.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Easier Shifted Signal

prompt_blocks.text: For $p(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $q(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-4)$, which convolution form makes the overlap setup simpler?

choice_blocks.text: Use $\int p(\tau)q(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, because the one-sided exponential should stay fixed and the finite pulse should move with $t$.
Use $\int q(\tau)p(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, because swapping is the better choice for every convolution.
Use $\int q(\tau)p(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, because $q(\tau)$ keeps the finite support $1\le \tau\le 4$ fixed and $p(t-\tau)$ is the shifted one-sided factor.
Use $\int p(\tau)q(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, because the exponential formula determines which factor should be fixed.
Use either form with no preference, because commutativity makes the support setup identical.

questions.correct_answer: Use $\int q(\tau)p(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, because the finite support of $q$ stays fixed in $\tau$ while the one-sided factor $p$ is shifted.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $p(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ is one-sided, while $q(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-4)$ has finite support from $1$ to $4$. The simpler setup keeps that finite interval fixed as $q(\tau)$ and shifts the one-sided factor as $p(t-\tau)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $a(t)=u(t+2)-u(t-1)$ and $b(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, which convolution form makes the overlap setup simpler?

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds After Swapping the Factors

prompt_blocks.text: After swapping, suppose the fixed factor is nonzero for $0\le \tau\le 3$, and the shifted factor is nonzero when $\tau\le t$. For $0<t<3$, what are the convolution bounds?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Intersect the fixed support $0\le \tau\le 3$ with the shifted condition $\tau\le t$. On the region $0<t<3$, the value $t$ lies inside the fixed interval, so the overlap runs from $0$ to $t$.

prompt_blocks.text: After swapping, suppose the fixed factor is nonzero for $1\le \tau\le 4$, and the shifted factor is nonzero when $t-\tau-1\ge 0$. For $5<t<7$, what are the convolution bounds?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First rewrite the shifted one-sided condition as $\tau\le t-1$. On the region $5<t<7$, we have $t-1>4$, so that shifted condition includes the entire fixed interval $1\le \tau\le 4$.
